steps.prompt: In VR, your hands ARE the controller.
steps.sub: The thing that makes VR feel magical isn't the visuals — it's reaching out and grabbing something. By the end you'll know exactly what it takes to make a virtual object grabbable, throwable, and touchable.

steps.prompt: You want the user to be able to pick up a virtual mug. What does the mug need?

options.t: Just a nice 3D model — VR makes everything grabbable automatically
A grab-interactable component plus a Rigidbody, so hands can latch on and physics can take over
A brighter material so the user can see it

steps.why: A model is just geometry — the engine has no idea it's holdable. A grab-interactable component is what tells the hand 'you can latch onto this,' and a Rigidbody is what gives it mass so that when you let go, it falls instead of floating. Together they turn a static model into something your hands can actually pick up.
hints: A 3D model alone is just a shape with no behaviour — something has to say 'this is grabbable.'
And once you let go, what makes it fall? Think physics.

steps.prompt: The 3 ingredients of a grabbable object.
steps.sub: Tap each card. Miss one and the grab feels broken.

cards.b: The headset knows where your real hands are and shows them in the scene. This is the input.
A component on the object that says 'a hand can latch onto me' and handles the attach when you grip.
Gives the object mass and gravity, so when you release it, it falls, bounces, and can be thrown.

steps.prompt: Which feature does each behaviour come from?
steps.sub: Tap an item, then a bin.

items.t: Your real hand appears and moves in the scene
The ball sticks to your palm when you close your grip
The ball flies in an arc and bounces when you throw it
The controller buzzes the instant you touch the ball

hints: Tracking is about SEEING your hands; the interactable is about LATCHING ON.
Flying-and-bouncing is physics; the buzz is the feedback in your hand.

steps.prompt: A grab with no feedback feels fake. What makes virtual touch feel physical?
steps.sub: This is the cheapest upgrade in all of VR.

options.t: A short haptic buzz in the controller the moment you touch or grab
A loud sound effect every time

steps.why: Haptics — a tiny vibration in the controller — is what closes the loop between seeing and feeling. When the buzz fires the instant your hand meets the object, your brain reads it as a real touch. It's one line of code, it costs almost nothing, and it's the difference between 'a floating model' and 'a thing I touched.'
hints: Touch in real life has a feeling. What can the controller produce that mimics that?
It's not visual and it's not audio — it's something you feel in your hand.

steps.prompt: Walk a single throw through, step by step.
steps.sub: Tap the events in the order they happen when a user grabs and throws a ball.
chips: You release — the Rigidbody takes the hand's velocity and the ball flies
Your tracked hand reaches the ball
The ball lands and bounces with physics
You grip — the grab-interactable attaches the ball and a haptic buzz fires
hints: Nothing happens until your hand actually reaches the ball.
Grab, then throw, then land — physics only takes over after you let go.

steps.prompt: Trace a full grab-and-throw with all four features working together.
steps.sub: Pick the next move at each turn. The log fills in as you go.
steps.goal: Let the user pick up a ball, feel it, throw it, and watch it bounce.

turns.situation: The ball sits on a table. The user reaches toward it with a tracked hand.
turns.q: What feature is letting the user's hand appear and move?
turns.log: ✋ Hand tracking → user's hand reaches the ball

turns.situation: The hand closes on the ball and grips.
turns.q: Two things should happen at once. Which is it?
options: The grab-interactable attaches the ball AND a haptic buzz confirms the touch
Nothing — wait for a button press
turns.log: 🤝 Grab interactable → ball attaches  ·  📳 Haptic buzz → touch confirmed

turns.situation: The user swings their arm and opens their hand to release.
turns.q: What gives the ball its flight?
options: The Rigidbody inherits the hand's velocity and the ball flies in an arc
The ball stays frozen in mid-air
The hand keeps holding it forever
turns.log: ⚖️ Rigidbody → ball flies with the throw's velocity

turns.situation: The ball arcs across the room toward the floor.
options: Physics makes it bounce and settle — a believable throw
It teleports back to the hand
turns.log: ✅ Ball bounces and settles — grab→feel→throw complete.

hints: Match each moment to one of the four features: tracking, interactable, physics, haptics.
The buzz fires on grab; physics only takes over on release.

steps.sub: Tap each, then check all at once.

statements.t: Adding a Rigidbody is what lets a thrown object fly and bounce realistically.
statements.why: True. The Rigidbody gives the object mass and gravity and inherits your hand's velocity on release — that's what makes a throw feel real.

statements.t: Haptic feedback is expensive and only worth it for big-budget apps.
statements.why: False. A haptic buzz is roughly one line of code and almost free to run — yet it's one of the biggest immersion upgrades you can add. Beginners should use it everywhere.

statements.t: A 3D model becomes grabbable on its own, with no extra components.
statements.why: False. A raw model is just geometry. It needs a grab-interactable to latch onto a hand and a Rigidbody for physics before it's actually grabbable.
